name: Loops and Functions
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: Loop with enumerate, zip, break and continue, then write functions with defaults, scope, pure logic and first recursion.

lesson.intro: Loops repeat work and functions package work under a name so you can reuse it. Together they are most of what any program is. This lesson covers looping the Pythonic way with enumerate and zip, steering loops with break, continue and else, nested loops, writing functions with parameters, defaults and return values, where variables live, why pure functions are easier to trust, and your first look at recursion.
objectives: Loop over sequences with for, enumerate and zip, and steer loops with break, continue and else
Predict how many times nested loops run and stop them cleanly
Write functions that take positional, default and keyword arguments and return values
Explain local and global scope and keep functions pure where possible
Trace a simple recursive function through its base case and recursive case

sections.title: Looping over anything: for, enumerate and zip
sections.body:
You have a list of names to print numbered 1, 2, 3, or two lists, names and scores, that line up position by position. Python's `for` loop plus two small helpers handle both without any index arithmetic.

A `for` loop works on any **iterable**: a list, a string (one character at a time), a `range`, a dictionary (its keys) and much more. The loop variable is simply bound to each item in turn.

`range(start, stop, step)` produces numbers lazily, so `range(1_000_000)` doesn't build a million-item list. It stops before `stop`, which is exactly what indexes need: `range(len(items))` gives every valid index.

You rarely need `range(len(...))`, though:
- `enumerate(items)` gives `(index, item)` pairs, so `for i, name in enumerate(names):` has both. `enumerate(names, start=1)` counts from 1 for human-friendly numbering.
- `zip(a, b)` walks two or more iterables side by side, giving `(a_item, b_item)` pairs. It stops at the shortest one and silently drops the extras, so check lengths when they must match. Python 3.10 and later accept `zip(a, b, strict=True)`, which raises an error instead.
- `reversed(items)` walks backwards, and `sorted(items)` walks in sorted order without changing the list.

To loop over a dictionary's keys and values together, use `for key, value in d.items():`.

Building a new list with a loop is so common that Python has a shortcut, the **list comprehension**: `[s * 2 for s in scores if s > 80]` means "for each s in scores, if s > 80, keep s * 2". It's the same loop written inside brackets. Use it for simple transformations and filters, and switch back to a normal loop when the logic needs more than one line. Intermediate Python covers comprehensions in depth.

Choose `for` whenever you know what you are looping over, and keep `while` for loops that run until something changes.
sections.pitfall: Assuming zip checks lengths. If one list is shorter, zip quietly stops early and the extra items vanish from your results.

activity.title: Print a numbered receipt
activity.prompt: The range(len(...)) loop works but is clumsy. Try enumerate(zip(items, prices), start=1): it yields pairs like (1, ('coffee', 3.5)), which you can unpack as i, (item, price). Format each price with :.2f.

props.code:
items = ["coffee", "bagel", "juice"]
prices = [3.5, 2.25, 4.0]

for i in range(len(items)):
    print(items[i], prices[i])
props.task: Make the program print exactly three lines: 1. coffee $3.50, then 2. bagel $2.25, then 3. juice $4.00

check.question: What does [c.upper() for c in "abc"] produce?
check.explanation: Square brackets make a list comprehension, which always builds a list, not a tuple. It loops over each character and uppercases it, giving three items, and it doesn't join them into one string.

sections.title: Steering loops: break, continue and else
sections.body:
You're scanning orders for the first one over $100, and once you find it there's no point checking the rest. Or you're processing lines of a file and want to skip the blank ones. `break` and `continue` handle exactly these.
- `break` ends the loop immediately. Execution carries on with the first line after the loop.
- `continue` skips the rest of the current pass and jumps to the next item (in a `while` loop, back to the condition check).

Both affect only the innermost loop they are in.

A common shape for "repeat until" is `while True:` with a `break` inside. It reads well when the exit condition is only known in the middle of the loop body, such as asking again until the input is valid. Make sure every path eventually reaches the `break`.

Loops also have an `else` clause, which surprises people: it runs when the loop finishes normally, without hitting `break`. That makes it a clean way to say "searched everything and didn't find it" without a separate flag variable. Read it as "no break".

One rule saves a lot of pain: don't add or remove items in a list while you are looping over it. Removing an item shifts everything after it one place left, but the loop's internal position still moves forward, so the next item gets skipped. Loop over a copy (`for n in nums[:]:`) or, better, build a new list of the items you want to keep.

Stopping early isn't only tidier, it's faster. A search that breaks at the first match does, on average, half the work of one that checks every item, and that difference grows with the data.
sections.pitfall: Removing items from a list while looping over it skips items. Loop over a copy such as `nums[:]`, or build a new list instead.

activity.title: Stop at the first match
activity.prompt: Run it and look at the check count: the loop keeps going after it has already found the name. Add a break in the right place so the search stops at the match.

props.task: Make the loop stop as soon as it finds the name, so the program prints exactly: found cy after 3 checks

check.question: In the first loop, what would print if break were replaced with continue?
check.explanation: With continue, 0 is skipped instead of ending the loop, and the odd numbers 7 and 9 are skipped as well. The loop goes on to reach 2, so 4 and 2 print.

sections.title: Nested loops
sections.body:
A seating chart has rows and seats, a spreadsheet has rows and columns, and comparing every student with every other student means pairs. Whenever data has two dimensions, or you need combinations, you get a loop inside a loop.

The inner loop runs completely for each pass of the outer loop. With an outer loop of 3 passes and an inner loop of 4, the inner body runs 3 times 4 = 12 times. That multiplication is worth noticing: nested loops over the same n items do about n times n work, written O(n^2). For 100 items that's 10,000 steps, which is fine. For a million items it's a trillion, which is why interviewers ask whether a nested loop can become a single pass with a dictionary or a set.

Common nested patterns:
- Grids: `for row in grid:` then `for cell in row:`.
- All pairs: `for i in range(n):` then `for j in range(i + 1, n):`, which visits each pair once and never pairs an item with itself.
- Tables: the outer loop picks a row, the inner loop builds that row's text, and the outer loop prints it.

`break` and `continue` only affect the innermost loop. To stop both loops when you find what you are looking for, the cleanest fix is to put the loops in a function and `return` from the inner one. A flag variable checked by the outer loop also works but is clumsier.

When the inner loop's range depends on the outer variable, as in `for j in range(i)`, count carefully: the inner loop runs 0 times, then 1, then 2, and so on. Writing a small table of i and j values is the reliable way to trace these.
sections.pitfall: Expecting `break` in the inner loop to stop the outer loop too. It only exits the innermost loop; return from a function to stop both.

activity.title: Build a multiplication table
activity.prompt: Add an inner loop over the columns. print(value, end=" ") keeps values on one line, and an empty print() after the inner loop ends the row.

props.task: Print four rows with values separated by spaces: 1 2 3 4, then 2 4 6 8, then 3 6 9 12, then 4 8 12 16.

check.question: How many times does the inner body run in for i in range(3): for j in range(5): ...?
check.explanation: The inner loop runs all 5 passes for each of the 3 outer passes, so 3 times 5 = 15. Adding the counts (8) is the usual mistake.

sections.title: Functions: parameters, arguments and return
sections.body:
Every program past a few dozen lines repeats itself: the same calculation, the same formatting, the same check. Functions give a piece of logic a name, so you write it once, test it once and call it anywhere.

`def name(parameters):` defines a function. **Parameters** are the names in the definition; **arguments** are the values you pass when calling. When you call `area(3, 4)`, Python binds `width = 3` and `height = 4` and runs the body. Like any assignment, that binds names to the caller's objects, so a function can change a list it receives.

`return` does two things: it ends the function immediately and hands a value back to the caller. Code after a `return` in the same block never runs, and a `return` inside a loop exits the loop and the function together. A function that ends without `return` returns `None`.

That leads to the most common function bug: printing instead of returning. `print` shows text to a person, and the caller gets nothing back. If the caller needs the result (to store it, compare it or pass it on), you must `return` it. A good default is that functions return values and only the top level of the program prints.

A function can return several values by returning a tuple, `return low, high`, and the caller unpacks it: `low, high = min_max(nums)`.

**Guard clauses** keep functions flat: handle the special cases first and return early, then write the main logic without nesting it inside an `else`.

Document what a function does with a **docstring**, a string literal on the first line of the body. Editors and `help(name)` display it. A good docstring says what goes in, what comes out and anything surprising.
sections.pitfall: A function that prints its result instead of returning it. It looks right when you run it, but the caller receives None.

activity.title: Write a password check
activity.prompt: Use a guard clause for the length, then loop over the characters: ch.isdigit() tells you whether a character is a digit. Return as soon as you know the answer, and don't print inside the function.

props.code:
def is_valid_password(pw):
    # Return True if pw has at least 8 characters and contains a digit.
    # Otherwise return False.
    pass


print(is_valid_password("hunter2"))
print(is_valid_password("correcthorse"))
print(is_valid_password("battery9staple"))
props.task: Make the function return the right bool so the program prints False, False, True.

check.question: Which statement about return is true?
choices: The lines after a return statement still run before the function ends
return ends the function and hands a value back to the caller
return prints its value on the screen
Every function must contain a return statement
check.explanation: Once return runs, the function stops and the caller receives the value. return doesn't print anything, and a function without return is allowed: it returns None.

sections.title: Default and keyword arguments
sections.body:
A function that formats prices usually wants a dollar sign and two decimals, but occasionally euros or no decimals. Default and keyword arguments let one function cover the common case simply and the rare case clearly.

A **default value** makes a parameter optional: `def price(amount, symbol="$", decimals=2):`. Callers can leave it out and the default is used. Parameters with defaults must come after those without, so `def f(a=1, b):` is a SyntaxError.

When calling, you can pass arguments by position or by name. **Keyword arguments** such as `price(5, decimals=0)` make calls self-documenting and let you skip earlier optional parameters. Positional arguments must come before keyword ones in a call, and passing a name the function doesn't have raises TypeError.

The famous trap: default values are evaluated **once**, when the `def` line runs, not on every call. With a mutable default like `items=[]`, every call that relies on the default shares the same list, so values from one call leak into the next. The standard fix is a `None` default and creating the list inside the function.

Two more tools show up in real code:
- `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, and `**kwargs` collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. `print()` itself uses this idea to accept any number of values.
- A bare `*` in the parameter list makes everything after it keyword-only: `def connect(host, *, timeout=10):` must be called as `connect("db", timeout=5)`. Library authors use this for options whose meaning would be unclear as a bare number.

The full order in a definition is: regular parameters, parameters with defaults, `*args`, keyword-only parameters, then `**kwargs`.
sections.code:
def price(amount, symbol="$", decimals=2):
    return f"{symbol}{amount:.{decimals}f}"

print(price(5))                   # $5.00
print(price(5, "€"))              # €5.00
print(price(5, decimals=0))       # $5

def add_tag(tag, tags=None):      # None, not [], as the default
    if tags is None:
        tags = []
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags

print(add_tag("a"), add_tag("b")) # ['a'] ['b']

def total(*args, **kwargs):
    print(args, kwargs)

total(1, 2, tax=0.2)              # (1, 2) {'tax': 0.2}
sections.pitfall: Using a mutable default such as `[]` or `{}`. It is created once and shared by every call, so default to None and create the list inside the function.

check.question: Why is def f(items=[]) risky?
choices: Python forbids lists as default values
The list is copied on every call, which is slow
items is always None inside the function
The default list is created once and shared by every call that uses it
check.explanation: Defaults are evaluated once, when the function is defined. Every call that relies on the default appends to the same list, so values from earlier calls leak into later ones. Python allows it, which is why it is a trap rather than an error.

sections.title: Scope: where variables live
sections.body:
You set `total = 0` at the top of a script, change `total` inside a function, and the outside `total` doesn't move. Or the function crashes with UnboundLocalError. Both come from Python's scope rules.

**Scope** is the region of code where a name is visible. Each function call gets its own **local scope**, created when the call starts and thrown away when it ends. Names assigned at the top level of a file live in the **global scope**.

When Python looks up a name, it searches in this order, called LEGB:
- Local: names assigned in the current function, including its parameters.
- Enclosing: names in any function this one is nested inside.
- Global: names at the top level of the module.
- Built-in: names Python provides, such as `len` and `print`.

The key rule: if a function **assigns** to a name anywhere in its body, that name is local everywhere in that function. That's why `counter = counter + 1` inside a function fails: the right side reads the local counter before it has a value. Reading a global without assigning to it is fine, and the value is looked up when the function runs, not when it was defined.

You can opt out with `global counter` (or `nonlocal` for an enclosing function's variable), but treat that as a last resort. Functions that change globals are hard to test and reason about, because their behavior depends on everything else that touched the global. Pass values in as parameters and hand results back with `return` instead.

Loops don't create a scope in Python: the loop variable still exists after the loop, holding its last value. JavaScript's `let` is block scoped, but Python has no block scope.

Shadowing is a related trap: naming a variable `list`, `sum` or `max` hides the built-in for the rest of that scope, so a later call to it fails with a confusing TypeError.
sections.code:
x = "global"

def show():
    x = "local"           # assignment makes x local to show
    print(x)

show()                    # local
print(x)                  # global

rate = 2
def scale(n):
    return n * rate       # only read, so this is the global rate
rate = 3
print(scale(5))           # 15: looked up at call time

for i in range(3):
    pass
print(i)                  # 2: loop variables outlive the loop

def increment(counter):   # better than a global: take the value in
    return counter + 1    # and hand the new value back
count = increment(0)
print(count)              # 1
sections.pitfall: Naming a variable `list`, `max` or `sum`. It shadows the built-in, and a later call such as `list("abc")` fails with TypeError: 'list' object is not callable.

check.question: A global variable total exists. A function runs total = 5 and returns. What happens to the global total?
choices: Nothing; the function created its own local total
check.explanation: Assignment inside a function creates a local variable unless the function declares global total. The global keeps its old value.

sections.title: Pure functions and functions as values
sections.body:
Two functions both compute an order total. One takes the prices and returns the total. The other reads a global cart, applies a discount stored in another global, prints the result and saves it to a file. The first can be tested in one line; the second needs the whole program set up first.

A **pure function** always returns the same output for the same inputs and has no **side effects**: it doesn't print, write files, change globals or mutate its arguments. Pure functions are easy to test (call it, check the result), easy to reuse and safe to call in any order. Real programs need side effects, of course, but the good habit is to keep the core logic pure and push printing, input and saving to the edges.

Signs a function is not pure:
- It reads or changes a global variable.
- It mutates an argument, such as appending to a list it was given.
- It prints, reads input, touches files or the network, or uses the current time or random numbers.

Functions are values in Python. A function name without parentheses refers to the function object itself, so you can store it in a variable, put it in a list or pass it to another function. `sorted(words, key=len)` passes the `len` function, and `sorted` calls it on each word to decide the order.

For a short function you only need once, a **lambda** writes it inline: `lambda p: p[1]` is a function that takes p and returns p[1]. Lambdas are limited to a single expression, so anything longer deserves a named `def`.

Functions that take or return other functions are called higher-order functions. You've already used several: `sorted`, `max` and `min` all accept `key=`.
sections.code:
# Not pure: depends on and changes the outside world
cart_total = 0
def add_to_total(price):
    global cart_total
    cart_total += price
    print("Total is now", cart_total)

# Pure: same inputs, same output, no side effects
def order_total(prices, discount=0):
    return sum(prices) * (1 - discount)

print(order_total([10, 20], 0.1))     # 27.0

words = ["kiwi", "fig", "banana"]
print(sorted(words, key=len))         # ['fig', 'kiwi', 'banana']

pairs = [("b", 2), ("a", 3), ("c", 1)]
print(max(pairs, key=lambda p: p[1])) # ('a', 3)

shout = str.upper                     # a function stored in a variable
print(shout("hey"))                   # HEY
sections.pitfall: Writing `key=len()` instead of `key=len`. With parentheses you call the function immediately (here a TypeError); without them you pass the function itself.

activity.title: Make a function pure
activity.prompt: apply_curve reads two globals, changes the scores list in place and prints. Rewrite it to take scores and curve as parameters and return a new list, then do the printing outside the function. The original list should survive unchanged.

props.code:
scores = [72, 88, 95]
curve = 5

def apply_curve():
    for i in range(len(scores)):
        scores[i] = scores[i] + curve
    print(scores)

apply_curve()
print(scores)
props.task: Print the curved list and then the untouched original: [77, 93, 100] on the first line and [72, 88, 95] on the second.

check.question: Why are pure functions easier to test?
choices: Their output depends only on their arguments, so calling them with known inputs and checking the result is enough
They run faster than other functions
Python checks them for errors before the program runs
They can never raise an exception
check.explanation: No hidden state means no setup: the same arguments always give the same result. Purity says nothing about speed, and a pure function can still raise, for example on a division by zero.

sections.title: Recursion: functions that call themselves
sections.body:
How many files are in a folder, counting everything inside its subfolders and their subfolders? You don't know how deep it goes, so no fixed number of nested loops can answer it. But the question contains a smaller copy of itself: the count for a folder is its own files plus the count for each subfolder. A function that calls itself, **recursion**, matches that shape exactly.

Every recursive function has two parts:
- A **base case**: an input small enough to answer directly, with no further calls. An empty list sums to 0, the factorial of 1 is 1, and a folder with no subfolders has just its own files.
- A **recursive case**: shrink the problem, call the function on the smaller version and combine the result. Each call must move toward the base case.

When a function calls itself, Python pauses the current call and starts a new one with its own local variables. The paused calls stack up on the **call stack** and finish in reverse order as each gets its answer back. Tracing `factorial(3)`: it waits for `factorial(2)`, which waits for `factorial(1)`, which returns 1. Then 2 * 1 = 2 comes back, and finally 3 * 2 = 6.

If the base case is missing or never reached, the calls never stop. Python protects itself with a recursion limit (1000 calls deep by default) and raises RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded. When you see that, check that every path reaches a base case.

Recursion isn't always the best tool. A simple loop is clearer and faster for summing a flat list, and naive recursion can repeat work enormously: computing Fibonacci numbers as `fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)` recomputes the same values again and again. Recursion shines for naturally nested data such as folders, trees, JSON and nested lists, and it's the foundation of the tree, backtracking and dynamic programming patterns in the interview topics.
sections.pitfall: A base case the recursive calls can skip past, such as checking `n == 0` while subtracting 2 from an odd number. Prefer a check like `n <= 0`.

activity.title: Watch the call tree grow
activity.prompt: Step through fib(5) and count how many times fib(2) gets computed from scratch. Then switch memoization on and compare the total number of calls: remembering answers turns repeated branches into instant lookups.

check.question: What happens when a recursive function's base case is never reached?
choices: It returns None after the first call
Python spots it before running and raises SyntaxError
It keeps calling itself until Python raises RecursionError
It loops forever without ever raising an error
check.explanation: Each call adds a frame to the call stack. Python stops the runaway at its recursion limit, about 1000 frames by default, with RecursionError. Nothing is checked before running, because whether the base case is reached depends on the values.

keyTerms.definition: Anything a for loop can walk through: lists, strings, ranges, dictionaries, files and more.
Wraps an iterable to yield (index, item) pairs; start= sets the first index.
Walks several iterables in step, yielding tuples, and stops at the shortest.
Ends the innermost loop immediately; a loop's else clause is skipped.
Skips the rest of the current pass and moves to the next one.
What a function hands back to its caller; None when there is no return.
A parameter with a value used when the caller leaves it out; evaluated once, at definition time.
An argument passed by parameter name, such as price(5, decimals=0).
The names a function assigns; they exist only during that call. Lookup order is LEGB.
A function whose output depends only on its inputs and that has no side effects.
A small anonymous function written inline, limited to a single expression.
A function calling itself on a smaller problem until it reaches a base case.

summary: Loop over items directly; use enumerate for indexes and zip for parallel lists, which stops at the shortest.
break exits the innermost loop, continue skips to the next pass, and a loop's else runs only when no break happened.
Nested loops multiply their work; return from a function to stop both loops at once.
Functions hand results back with return, and mutable defaults are shared, so default to None.
Assigning inside a function makes a name local; prefer parameters and return values over globals, and keep core logic pure.
Recursion needs a base case and a recursive case that moves toward it.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who is new to programming how factorial(3) works step by step using the call stack, and what goes wrong if you forget the base case.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 3 (3 and 6) are skipped by continue. 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 are added, giving 19. When n reaches 8, break ends the loop, so 8 and 9 are never added.

questions.question: How many lines does this print?
questions.explanation: break only exits the inner loop. For each i, the inner loop prints i and 0, then breaks when j is 1, and the outer loop carries on. That gives three lines, not one.
questions.concept: break exits only the innermost loop

questions.question: Complete the loop so it prints a and b and skips the empty string.
questions.explanation: continue skips the print for the empty string and moves on to b. break would end the loop before b, and pass does nothing, so an empty line would print. return is only valid inside a function.

questions.question: This should remove every even number, but it prints [4, 5]. Why?
choices: Removing items from the list being looped over shifts the rest, so some are skipped; loop over a copy such as nums[:]
remove() deletes items by index, not by value
n % 2 == 0 is true for odd numbers
The for loop runs only once, because nums changes length
questions.explanation: After 2 is removed, 4 shifts into position 0, but the loop moves on to position 1, which now holds 5, so 4 is never checked. Looping over nums[:] avoids this, or build a new list with [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 1].
questions.concept: changing a list while looping over it

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
def double(n):
    print(n * 2)

result = double(5)
print(result)
questions.explanation: Calling double(5) prints 10. The function has no return, so result is None, and the second print shows None. To use the value later, return n * 2 instead of printing it.
questions.concept: a function without return gives None

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: return ends the function the moment it runs, even in the middle of a loop. 3 and 7 are skipped, 8 is returned, and 10 is never checked. return -1 only runs if the loop finishes without finding an even number.

questions.question: Why does this crash with a TypeError?
questions.code:
def average(nums):
    total = sum(nums)
    avg = total / len(nums)

score = average([80, 90])
print(score + 5)
choices: sum() can't add a list of ints
average computes avg but never returns it, so score is None and None + 5 fails
avg is a float, and floats can't be added to ints
len(nums) is 0, so the division fails
questions.explanation: Without return avg, the function returns None, and the error comes from score + 5 outside the function. Floats and ints add fine, and the list has two items, so the division works.

questions.question: What is the difference between returning a value and printing it?
questions.answer: print shows text on the screen and gives the caller nothing back (the function returns None). return hands a value back to the caller, which can store it or use it in more calculations. A function can print without returning and return without printing.
questions.explanation: Mixing these up is the most common reason a function's result turns out to be None.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: history=[] is created once, when def runs. All three calls append to that same list, so the third call sees three items. Each call does not get a fresh empty list.

questions.question: Complete the check so each call without a history argument gets a fresh list.
questions.explanation: None is the placeholder default, so test for it with is None and create the list inside the function. history is [] is always False, because [] builds a new list each time, so the list is never created and append fails.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: *args gathers the positional arguments into a tuple, which prints with parentheses. **kwargs gathers the keyword arguments into a dict. Because the function has **kwargs, the keyword unit is accepted instead of raising TypeError.

questions.question: Python refuses to run this file at all. Why?
choices: f-strings can't be returned from a function
greet must be called with positional arguments
A parameter without a default can't follow one with a default; put name first
questions.explanation: This is a SyntaxError, found before anything runs. Parameters without defaults must come before those with defaults: def greet(name, greeting="Hi"). Calling with a keyword argument is fine once the definition is fixed.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
x = 5

def change():
    x = 99
    return x

change()
print(x)
questions.explanation: x = 99 inside change() creates a local variable, so the global x is never touched and still holds 5. change() did return 99, but nothing stored it.
questions.concept: assignment inside a function is local

questions.question: Calling increment() raises UnboundLocalError. Why?
questions.code:
counter = 0

def increment():
    counter = counter + 1
    return counter

increment()
choices: Assigning to counter inside the function makes it local, so reading it on the right side fails before it has a value
counter must be declared with a type first
Functions can never read variables defined outside them
questions.explanation: Because the function assigns to counter, Python treats counter as local throughout the function, and counter + 1 reads that local before it is set. Functions can read globals as long as they don't also assign to them. A cleaner design takes counter as a parameter and returns counter + 1.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
rate = 2

def scale(n):
    return n * rate

rate = 3
print(scale(5))
questions.explanation: scale() never assigns to rate, so rate refers to the global, and Python looks it up when the function is called, not when it is defined. By the time of the call rate is 3, so the result is 5 * 3 = 15.
questions.concept: globals are read at call time

questions.question: Two nested loops search a grid for a value. What is the cleanest way to stop both loops as soon as it is found?
choices: Write break twice on the same line
Use continue in the inner loop instead
Move the loops into a function and return when you find it
Reassign the outer loop variable to end the outer loop
questions.explanation: return leaves the whole function, and with it every loop inside. break only exits the innermost loop, continue keeps looping, and reassigning a for loop's variable doesn't stop it, because the next pass rebinds it.

questions.question: What two parts does every recursive function need, and what does each do?
questions.answer: A base case, which answers a small enough input directly without recursing, and a recursive case, which calls the function on a smaller version of the problem and combines the result. Every recursive call must move closer to the base case.
questions.explanation: Without a reachable base case, the calls pile up until Python raises RecursionError.

questions.question: Why does this raise TypeError?
choices: Keyword arguments must come before positional ones
The function has no parameter named type, so the keyword is unexpected; call make_tag("Hello", tag="h1")
questions.explanation: A keyword argument must match a parameter name exactly, so Python raises TypeError: make_tag() got an unexpected keyword argument 'type'. The positional argument correctly comes first.

questions.question: Put these parameters in the order Python requires in one def line.
questions.explanation: Regular parameters come first, then ones with defaults, then *args. Anything after *args can only be passed by keyword, and **kwargs always comes last: def f(name, greeting="Hi", *args, loud=False, **kwargs).

bump()

questions.question: Put the scopes in the order Python searches them when it looks up a name.
items: Enclosing: functions this one is nested inside
Built-in: names like len and print
questions.explanation: This is the LEGB rule. The first scope that has the name wins, which is why a local variable called len hides the built-in len inside that function.

questions.question: Which of these functions is pure?
choices: def area(w, h): return w * h
def next_id(): global last; last += 1; return last
questions.explanation: area depends only on its arguments and changes nothing. add_item mutates its argument, log_total prints (a side effect), and next_id reads and changes a global, so it returns something different on every call.

questions.question: This crashes with RecursionError. Why?
questions.code:
def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:
        print("liftoff")
        return
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 2)

countdown(5)
choices: print can't be called inside a recursive function
n goes 5, 3, 1, -1 and skips 0, so the base case never runs; use if n <= 0
countdown must return a value on every path
A function can't call itself before its definition has finished
questions.explanation: Stepping down by 2 from an odd number never lands on 0, so the calls go on into negative numbers until Python's recursion limit stops them. A base case of n <= 0 catches every path.
